  • Industry observers note that before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out. They can save your training, and I swear, they can be a ton of fun—really. Between the engaging, interactive streaming treadmill classes, and the ability to strip down to your skivvies and have no one see you sweat, it’s the perfect accompaniment to your marathon training, interval workouts, and even steady, zone 2 workouts. All from the comfort of your own home. And did you know that with many insurance intends, you can pay for your treadmill with FSA dollars? That’s a solid fiscal choice, right there.

Recent findings suggest that there are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been. They have more features, use less electricity, and are more versatile than ever before. Some are virtually personal trainers in and of themselves.

We’re in the process of testing a few latest models, and we’ve just added the Urevo CyberMega, which is the first treadmill designed specifically for marathon training. It’s pretty freaking sick, I cannot lie.

Looking for a more heavy-duty treadmill that can handle higher speeds, longer miles, and more complex training intends? See our guide for the best advanced treadmills, which cost more but offer more training features and sturdier builds.

There’s really something special about this machine. The NordicTrack Commercial 1750 treadmill hits that “Goldilocks-level” sweet spot with its cushioning—it’s responsive enough to save your joints without making your run feel like a slog or an unstable adventure. And with a 60-inch belt, even our tallest testers with their gazelle-like strides had plenty of room to stretch out and feel steady.

Our testers absolutely gushed over the treadmill’s sleek, streamlined design, especially the Z-shaped console with its high-perched 16-inch screen. It’s perfectly positioned for runners who like to stay close to the controls. While we wished the cup holders were a bit deeper for our oversized water bottles, the slim arms offered a surprisingly stable grip, even when our hands got a little… enthusiastic.

The 1750’s speed adjustments are pretty standard, going from 6 mph to a zippy 12 mph in 8 seconds. This is totally fine for 400- to 800-meter training, but for intense, quick-pickup speedwork, it’s not quite as snappy as some might like. Our testers did note one minor peeve: the lack of quick keys for 10 and 11 mph.

We practically insist you dive into NordicTrack’s iFit program for an out-of-this-world experience. Our testers found its ability to read and adjust their runs to be nothing short of revolutionary during testing. While the high horsepower motor and Bluetooth speakers do make the machine a bit boisterous, it’s not at all distracting when you’re walking with your headphones on.

Recent findings suggest that despite its daunting price tag, the 1750 is a total workhorse that will supercharge your runs—and it goes on sale often. The built-in Netflix feature is a godsend, making miles absolutely fly by, and that cushioning is pure magic for your joints. Bottom line: the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 is a fantastic all-around package and a top-notch investment for most runners.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Review.

Recent findings suggest that the Horizon T101 treadmill proves you don’t need a huge budget for a fantastic workout. At a sale price of just $600, this compact folding machine impressed us with consistent performance over weeks of testing. It’s a low-to-the-ground, 20- by 55-inch deck, ideal for casual runners 6 feet and under.

According to recent reports, the T101 boasts a three-zone running surface, offering extra cushioning where you land, less where you toe off, and a smooth transition in between for a supremely comfortable, low-impact ride. While it skips the fancy screens, its functionality shines. Connect to Strava or Peloton, or dive into workouts and courses via the free atZone app. Plus, there’s a perfect spot for your iPad to stream your favorite reveals!

The six built-in programs are straightforward, displaying calories burned, heart rate, distance, speed, and incline (up to 10 percent). While it can hit a 6-minute mile, be mindful: the speed and incline dials are sensitive—one haptic notch, not a full spin, increases your pace.

But you know what’s a real showstopper? The T101’s incredibly easy, one-step hydraulic fold. Just lift the back, and it zips up. To release, toe the center bar, and it gently lowers itself.

Recent findings suggest that for its price, the T101’s features are unbeatable. It’s not for marathoners or speed demons, but for everyone else, it’s a solid win.

Horizon’s 7.0 folding treadmill is a robust upgrade, boasting a spacious 60-inch deck perfect for long strides, though its 20-inch width might feel snug if your mind wanders. Cushioning is excellent for long runs, but expect some bounce when the incline exceeds 5 percent—so perhaps skip the speedy hill work.

According to recent reports, this machine is on the bulkier side, resembling a gym-quality unit, but its integrated features ensure easy setup. We loved the eye-level tablet holder, making streaming a breeze. Below, you’ll find a digital/manual console, fan, Bluetooth speakers, and two generously wide (if shallow) cup holders with room for your essentials.

According to recent reports, programming-wise, the 7.0 shines with its ability to link to Peloton, Apple Watch, and Samsung Galaxy watches, displaying calories and distance directly. Peloton classes synced smoothly, making transitions seamless.

A standout feature: knobs on the grips allow for effortless pace adjustments without breaking your stride. While there’s a subtle lag when decreasing speed, it’s barely noticeable at top speeds.

At around $1,000 on sale, this treadmill offers impressive value. Its blend of convenience and comfort makes it a winner. Pro tip: opt for white-glove delivery—this beast is heavy, and assembly is a pain!

Full Horizon 7.0 AT Treadmill Review.

Marathon training demands months of relentless mileage, a crap ton of structured workouts, and more consistency than most of us think we’re capable of. The Urevo CyberMega is a treadmill that claims to be built specifically for the rigors of that beast of blocks. In a market crowded with all-purpose machines designed to serve everyone from casual walkers to occasional joggers to high-mileage baddies, the CyberMega is thinking of the needs of marathon runners first.

Recent findings suggest that that marathon-focused idea makes the entire experience. Rather than treating running as just one feature among many, the CyberMega is designed around the realities of high-volume training. According to the brand, every aspect of the machine is intended to support athletes preparing for long-distance races, making it a notably different proposition from traditional fitness-focused treadmills.

There are marathon courses built into the app that control your ‘mill, there’s AI coaching to get you to your PR, and a fun competitive leaderboard where you are up against other consumers. This treadmill is made to keep your training going when you can’t get outside and also? To keep it exciting. It is honestly fairly impressive and a ton of fun to run on.

I was also impressed by how smooth the run is and how compact the machine is. It folds easily, stores without much hassle, and feels dang streamlined for a treadmill made to support hardcore training. That’s also the biggest drawback. If you’re over 6 feet tall, this is not the ‘mill for you with a 52-inch-long deck. But in spite of the short deck, it landed on this list is because it’s a wide-open area that doesn’t feel impeded by the bars.

In a recent development, the rotary knob is another nifty feature. It’s simple, responsive, and super convenient during workouts, and has speed and incline adjustments feeling smoother and more intuitive than traditional button-based controls or rocker dials. Overall, if you’re gonna be a world major chaser, you might want to think about chasing them on this ‘mill.

Got a few runners in the family, or you’re a high-mileage runner? The NordicTrack 2450 is a seriously solid folding treadmill that’s got your back. It’s built tough, has great cushioning, and a huge 22-by-60-inch running surface, so you can just run without worrying about comfort and stability.

The Z-shaped handlebar and crossbar design are super minimalist, keeping the console right there when you need it, and giving you plenty of room to stretch out at the front of the belt.

It has been revealed that you’ve got your standard speed and incline adjustments, and this baby can zoom from 6 to 14 mph in under 10 seconds—perfect for those quick interval bursts. It has those quick keys like the 1750, but sometimes it can be a little tricky to nail down specific speeds.

Recent findings suggest that where the NordicTrack really shines is its iFit programming. We’re talking thousands of workouts, even marathon courses! Yeah, it’s an extra cost, but seriously, it’s a huge motivator. And that big display? It’s awesome. You can pause your run to squeeze in some strength training or even stream your favorite shows.

According to recent reports, fair warning, though: putting this thing together is a beast, so you might want to call in a pro. And while it’s not super loud, it might be a bit disruptive if you’re trying to sneak in an early morning workout while everyone else is still snoozing.

The ProForm Carbon TLX is a robust and dependable treadmill, designed for those who appreciate solid performance over excessive features. Its simplicity allows for focused workouts, minimizing distractions so you can stay in tune with your run. While it offers connectivity for phones, tablets, and fitness apps like iFit, at its core, the Carbon TLX is a workhorse—a no-fuss machine ready for you to hop on, get your miles in, and hop off.

It has been revealed that the treadmill features a responsive and cushioned surface that offers a pleasant bounce at higher speeds. Our testers found that despite the softer feel, the generous 60- by 20-inch deck allowed for a natural stride. However, I did occasionally feel myself drawing closer to the front console, so if you prefer more forward space, a different model might be better suited.

According to recent reports, for speed enthusiasts, the Carbon TLX is a dream. It rapidly reaches its top speed of 12 mph, and manual buttons provide smooth transitions between speeds. The incline goes up to 12 percent, providing a challenging workout that feels surprisingly good, even uphill. A standout feature is the powerful fan, strategically placed to provide excellent airflow—a detail any woman who’s done the “lift the boobs to get air” maneuver will appreciate.

If you’re a first-time treadmill buyer or looking to stay within budget, the Carbon TLX offers exceptional value for its price.

Industry observers note that the Bowflex T9 treadmill brings a punch of fun and functionality to home workouts, making it a standout pick for casual runners and fitness fans alike. The red center line on the belt isn’t just for show—it helps wandering runners stay in their lane, so every jog feels more confident (and a little less wobbly). The running surface is firm and comfortable, with just enough pep to keep things lively, while the compact, foldable design slides neatly out of the way after your workout adventure.

Sources indicate that the controls and incline? Well, they’re not winning any races. Adjustments take their time, so interval chasers might grumble about holding down those buttons like they’re cranking up a jack-in-the-box. But the T9 redeems itself with robust app compatibility—it syncs up with Peloton, Zwift, and even Apple Watch for gadget lovers, and has an oversized tablet holder for serious streaming or stats-watching mid-run.

Weighing in with a 350-pound weight capacity, a quiet motor, and speed toggles at your fingertips, this treadmill turns everyday training into smooth sailing. It may not be a speed demon, but the T9’s thoughtful features combine comfort and tech for an overall enjoyable ride.

The Echelon Stride 6 is the treadmill I’ve kept at home after running over 1,200 miles on dozens of machines testing them for this article. It’s a solid, foldable treadmill that fits well in small spaces without feeling cramped. The larger-than-expected deck is 20.5 by 60 inches, giving plenty of room for a natural stride, even at my height of 6 feet. The deck provides firm cushioning that’s comfortable but not overly soft, which I definitely prefer for a closer to road-like feel.

The fold-flat design is a major bonus. The mill is stupid easy to tuck away under a bed or stand upright in a closet or—how I do it—up against a wall behind a curtain. That remarked, it’s heavy when folded upright, so moving it alone can be a pain. The treadmill has a powerful built-in fan and heart rate sensors, nice extras for longer sessions.

Overall, the Stride 6 isn’t flashy or cushioned like some high-end models, but it delivers a dependable run and great space-saving convenience. For a runner who values a firm deck, quiet motor, and compact footprint, it’s a practical choice that keeps me coming back.

Not everyone needs a treadmill for running, and we get that. Sometimes, what you need is access to movement and the ability to stay active all day long. Enter the Go Plus under-desk walking pad. It is the bridge between daily life and running.

I love using this walking pad when I am working. It’s calm and quiet, but allows me to keep my body and brain active when I'd otherwise be sedentary. It has a deck that is a wonderful size to fit under your standing desk, though I do think it could be just a teeny bit wider. It’s only about 50 pounds, and has wheels so you can maneuver it around your space easily. It’s remote-controlled for easy use, and best of all? You can store this gal vertically in your closet. (Just don’t forget about it in there!).

Each and every treadmill on this list has been thoroughly evaluated by our team of editors at Runner’s World. I have personally tested each and every ‘mill on this list. Additionally, we solicited input from other staff at our office, like News Editor Theo Kahler, who has a PR of 14:20 in the 5K.

Recent findings suggest that the team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly important factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

Recent findings suggest that apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

In a recent development, having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

Having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

The length of the deck is a trickier glitch. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

According to recent reports, if you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

Incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

Treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running plans and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

And perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

Industry observers note that motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

Recent findings suggest that speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

According to recent reports, we have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

Sources indicate that it’s predictable. Greer claims that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, fresh to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

It also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

There are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature demonstrates some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

When you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

In a recent development, you might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

You need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

According to recent reports, treadmills are a big piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most important safety factors before you purchase a newly introduced treadmill for your home.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and presently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

#68421. Latest Update: 3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1307 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling.
  • As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.
  • Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling. Our regular eating schedules shift around social gatherings, holiday menus influence our usual food choices, and staying hydrated can take more effort without higher temperatures to drive our thirst.

As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.

Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.

In a recent development, vitamin D deficiencies are common among athletes in winter, Maddie Alm, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Fueling Forward Sports Nutrition in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. That’s because shorter days and colder temperatures can mean less exposure to the sun’s UVB rays, which help our bodies produce vitamin D.

According to recent reports, alm explains that this vitamin not only supports strong bones, but also helps keep our immune and digestive systems functioning at their best. It plays an key role in brain health and mood, too. According to the National Institutes of Health, low blood levels of the vitamin have been associated with a higher risk of depression.

The Fix: Get outside daily to catch some sunshine, and focus on eating more vitamin D–rich foods, with the goal to consume 600 international units (IU) per day.

Good sources of vitamin D include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, tuna, salmon, egg yolk, and mushrooms. Some cereals and orange juices are also vitamin D–fortified. For reference, three ounces of salmon contain 450 IU, one cup of cow’s milk contains 180 IU, one large egg yolk contains 40 IU, and one cup of fortified cereal contains 40 IU.

Industry observers note that it’s a good idea, Alm adds, to check your levels through bloodwork once or twice a year and to consult a professional if your numbers come back low. If you have a hard time hitting your daily quota through food alone, you may benefit from taking a vitamin D supplement.

Runners can also overlook vitamin C intake this time of year, states Sakiko Minagawa, RD, a registered dietitian for the Division of Sports Medicine at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio and two-time Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, supports immune health, which is especially notable during cold and flu season.

In a recent development, our bodies also need vitamin C to produce collagen, a protein that’s essential for tissue growth and repair. “While vitamin C may not prevent you from outright getting sick, some research shows that it may decrease the duration of cold symptoms,” Minagawa explains.

It has been revealed that the Fix: Up your consumption of foods with vitamin C, such as bell peppers, citrus fruits, greens, and strawberries. Women should aim for 75 milligrams per day, while men should aim for 90 milligrams daily.

You’ll get about 210 milligrams from one large red or orange bell pepper, and 90 milligrams in a cup of raw strawberry halves—each of which achieves your recommended daily dose.

Because vitamin C helps with iron absorption, Minagawa suggests pairing the two whenever possible. Some meals she recommends are a spinach salad with strawberries, an omelet with spinach and red bell peppers, and tomato soup with lentils or black beans.

In the winter, you might not end your run with a dry mouth and sweat-soaked shirt like in the summer, but it’s still critical to hydrate. “Even when it’s cold, you still sweat,” claims Minagawa, which means you still need to replenish fluids throughout the day, as well as before and after a workout.

In a recent development, similarly, your midrun fueling and hydrating remain just as crucial for performance. It’s true: Tearing open an energy gel with gloved hands can pose a real challenge. But, if you’re doing long runs through the colder months, you still need to consume enough carbohydrates during your effort.

The Fix: Minagawa suggests carrying a water bottle that you can easily drink from and refill throughout the day. If you have a hard time sipping on plain water, remember that soups, broths, and hot chocolate can also help you stay hydrated—and can double as recovery fuel.

Industry observers note that don’t forget about fresh fruits and vegetables, either, as they can help with hydration. Some great in-season options that can contribute to your overall fluid intake include grapefruit, clementines, pomegranate, kiwi, squash, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, pears, kale, and cabbage.

During your winter long runs, experiment with fueling options other than energy gels and chews. Some great alternatives you can easily carry in a small plastic baggie include salted Medjool dates, boiled red potatoes, dried fruit, pretzels, and even candy.

Recent findings suggest that bad weather conditions, scant daylight hours, and more limited racing opportunities make winter a time for many athletes to dial back their training. Taking an off-season can benefit you in the long haul, but Minagawa encourages runners to still stay active—even if that means swapping some runs for walks, bike rides, easy swims, or elliptical sessions.

It has been revealed that you don’t want to depart from those year-round healthy habits, Brianna Butler, RD, a registered dietitian, co-owner of Stef & Bri Wellness in Texas, and former professional WNBA athlete, previously told Runner’s World. The same applies to your nutrition.

“The biggest mistake runners make is that, when it’s the off-season, they’re off everything—they say, ‘I’m not doing anything, I’m going to eat whatever’—they’re just winging it,” Butler says. “It shouldn’t be all or nothing. We want to make sure we’re nourishing our bodies well year-round.”.

If your training load changes significantly, pay closer attention to your hunger cues to make sure your nutrition matches your energy needs.

The Fix: Maintain a daily exercise routine you enjoy, prioritize nutrient-dense meals and snacks, and resist making drastic changes to your diet.

If you do find yourself feeling sluggish this time of year, it can be tempting to repent with cleanses, detoxes, and extreme exercise regimens. But such quick fixes rarely pay off in the long run, Alm warns, as they put you at risk for injury, burnout, and subpar seasons to come.

Alm says not to stress if you ditched your typical eating and training schedule for a few weeks and are feeling less energetic as a result. When you return to your usual healthy habits, your body will naturally find its sweet spot. “Trust the process and don’t panic,” Alm advises, because our bodies may change as we move through different training phases. “It is okay to not be at your leanest year-round.”.

Industry observers note that the smartest path forward? Do your best to move your body daily, fuel it with what it needs, and give yourself permission to rest when you’re tired. That way, you’ll find yourself feeling strong and ready to train hard again come spring.

It has been revealed that morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

In a recent development, A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

Our Go-To Beginner Running Shoe Got Mixed Reviews—Here’s Why the Brooks Ghost 18 Is Still Worth Considering

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • According to recent reports, our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost.
  • When we covered the Ghost 18’s release in May, our staff had already logged a few weeks of mileage in the shoe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, our usual go-to shoe recommendation for new runners has always been the Brooks Ghost. It’s the ideal trainer to choose when you’re overwhelmed with all the offerings out there, unsure where to start or which shoe is right for you. The Ghost was a part of the quintessential runner starter pack:.

But this year was different. When we covered the Ghost 18’s release in May, our staff had already logged a few weeks of mileage in the shoe. And the verdict was... mixed.

It’s been six months since that initial testing, and during that time, the brand’s cushier model, the Brooks Glycerin 23, surpassed the Ghost in terms of popularity and positive feedback. What it all came down to was fit.

Industry observers note that when we evaluate running shoes, we rate key attributes like weight, flexibility, and durability. Predictably, the Glycerin 23 scored a lower overall average score in weight compared to the Ghost 18 (the former is tenths of an ounce heavier than the Ghost). Other features between the shoes were relatively similar, except when it came to comfort. The Glycerin 23 received high scores, whereas the Ghost 18’s comfort was rated high by men and very low by women. The keyword here was “crammed.”.

In a recent development, “I had no cramming of my toes,” noted Glycerin 23 tester Maura Dalek. “My feet had plenty of room to move around in and kept my feet dry and cool.”.

Juxtapose this with Ghost 18 tester and Deputy Editor Mallory Creveling’s comment: “The length was great; the width not so much...[My] forefoot area [felt] crammed the more I ran.”.

It wasn’t just women testers who felt this version of the Ghost ran narrower than previous iterations. Art Director John Hamilton stated he would have felt comfier in a wider fit. Despite his discomfort, he still gave the Ghost 18 a high rating.

According to recent reports, like eating mushrooms or drinking a martini neat, sometimes running in a shoe is an acquired taste. While it’s not the advice I’d give to runners shopping for running shoes (“You’ll eventually love it. Really!”), it’s a pickle we sometimes allow ourselves to fall into: a model you’ve always liked and the newest one doesn’t feel the same, but you’re going to stick it out anyway.

So I asked testers what they thought of the Ghost 18 months later. Creveling remarked she gave the shoe several chances, and had maybe two pain-free runs in them.

But here’s where our testing is limited: The Ghost 18 is available in several widths, including narrow, wide, and extra wide. Our samples come in the standard width (B for women, D for men), and our testing pool includes runners of various foot shapes. Fit varies across brands, and yes, even from model to model.

Here’s one piece of gear advice I can’t emphasize enough (people in the back, do you hear me?): It’s key to try on a shoe and go for a test run in it first before making a commitment. Another underrated piece of advice is getting your foot measured to see if you need a narrower or wider width. Your feet change over time due to aging, life events, and gravity.

In a recent development, one tester who had no matter with the shoe’s fit had this to say: “High [score] overall for the latest edition of the Ghost. As an owner of previous Ghost models, this one is a worthy successor. Everything that makes the Ghost great as a daily trainer is present here—stability, durability, great on wet roads or loose gravel.” And on the fit? “Plenty of room in the toebox...Super comfortable.”.

In a recent development, runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate was also satisfied with the Ghost 18’s comfort. “Brooks continues to nail the fit,” he said. “It’s one of the reasons I love their shoes—no matter how a model evolves, I know I’m going to get a good wrap. Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

He is referring to the familiar touch points we know and love about Brooks shoes: a plush heel collar that fits securely around your ankle, a flat ribbed tongue that looks like the cuffs on a cozy knit sweater.

Though the shoe doesn’t pack as powerful a punch with DNA Loft v3 foam (nitrogen-infused EVA) compared to shoes with TPEE or PEBA, it’s a reliable mile muncher, making it worthy for logging those everyday workouts when you’re building toward a race or just getting started with running.

Recent findings suggest that at $150, the Ghost 18 is comparable to the $145 Upcoming Balance Ellipse. If you want a slightly heavier, cushier daily trainer that costs $175, go with the Glycerin 23. If you want a true Goldilocks shoe that’s slightly lighter with a generous amount of cushioning, go with the Ghost 18. Just consider your width options before buying!

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

The 5 Best Outdoor Saunas for Getting Your Sweat On in 2025

📅 06 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.
  • There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves.
  • We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any newly introduced supplement or exercise regimen.

Sources indicate that if you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

Sources indicate that according to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

Recent findings suggest that A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

The Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

Industry observers note that the choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the customers in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

Recent findings suggest that you can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

Sources indicate that the Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

One benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors notes that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

Industry observers note that the Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

According to recent reports, if you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael states.

Recent findings suggest that putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One big bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma claims. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”.

It has been revealed that depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

In a recent development, as for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”.

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

According to recent reports, “You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” states Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee indicates. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”.

Most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

In a recent development, given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

Sources indicate that the outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Recent findings suggest that many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung problems.

Recent findings suggest that the cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

It has been revealed that when investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.

It has been revealed that editor’s Note, November 18, 2026: Brooks has a mega sale going on right now. The Glycerin Flex, Adrenaline GTS 25, and Glycerin Max 2 are on discounts as high as 25% off. The Adrenaline GTS 26 is out now—we’ll be getting in feedback soon. All this is to say, better stock up on the 25 before it’s gone.

It has been revealed that in 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the organization started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

Sources indicate that since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

Gear Up for Training Season: Best Running Shorts ● Best Socks for Runners ● Best Running Watches.

According to recent reports, our team vets hundreds of shoes a year and distributes models to more than 250 local testers for evaluation. Shoe testers of different levels, ages, arch heights, and gait patterns log at least a hundred miles before submitting feedback on a shoe’s fit, feel, and ride. Keep returning for more updates as we make our way through 2026’s hottest Brooks releases.

All weights are based on men’s 9 and women’s 7 unless otherwise noted.

In a recent development, the Glycerin 23 knocked the Ghost 18 out of Best Overall this round. While the Ghost 18 is still on this list as Best Daily Trainer, we found during testing that the Glycerin 23 is more foot shape-friendly. Testers liked the broader platform and toe room, as well as the bouncy and supportive cushioning. The shoe is my go-to for daily training—but the long run is where it shines.

I usually grab a carbon-plate shoe for my long runs, especially when I’m less confident about being out on the road for two hours at the beginning of marathon training. But the Glycerin 23’s midsole upgrade convinced me to save my carbon shoes for race day. DNA Tuned is lighter than DNA Loft, the Glycerin’s previous foam, and delivers a springier ride. My legs feel fresh when I power down hills in the shoes. The energy return doesn’t make my double-digit runs feel like a crawl.

According to recent reports, the shoe is also available as the Glycerin GTS 23, the stability counterpart. I find the Glycerin GTS 23 slightly stiffer and firmer than the neutral model, but it’s a good choice for runners who need a little more support on their long runs if they’re prone to late-onset overpronation, or if they prefer denser cushioning underfoot.

According to recent reports, the Launch is a solid speedwork shoe for $120. It has the Hyperion Elite’s original DNA Flash v2 in the forefoot. The nitrogen-infused foam was what Brooks elite athletes relied on before the brand switched to DNA Gold PEBA.

Recent findings suggest that the Launch 12 is lightweight and narrow. Wide-foot runners will want to opt for a more accommodating speed shoe, like the Hyperion 3 on this list. All other runners who have a standard to narrow foot shape will appreciate this bargain shoe’s swiftness on the track and road.

“They felt light enough to rip off some faster-paced fartlek segments during the middle of a regular run, but still supportive enough to make it through a longer run,” remarked tester and Hyper Editor Ashley Tysiac.

For the first time, a Ghost’s midsole has PEBA—the soft and bouncy foam that once was reserved for marathon racing shoes is making its way into trainers. The new DNA Hype foam is a combination of PEBA and EVA, and the difference in ride is noticeable comparing it to the Ghost 18 (below).

It has been revealed that our testers liked the high energy return on their runs, causing them to favor the shoe for hard tempos and track workouts. The Ghost always hits the right marks for every kind of runner at every level—soft, supportive cushioning; all-encompassing comfort; not too light, not too heavy. However, testers were divisive with the Ghost 18’s key patch. The newly introduced jacquard engineered air mesh upper gives the Ghost a sporty meets street casual look. Even in the Ghost, which is a little more spartan for padding and luxury, it still wraps the foot well and feels good no matter how far I run.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Ghost 18 is a great trainer for newly introduced runners and those looking for a trusty workhorse to log daily mileage. However, in lieu of the Ghost 18, women and wide-foot runners may want to opt for our Best Overall, the Glycerin 23, for their daily training, instead.

Before you come at recommending an “illegal shoe” that goes well above World Athletics below-40mm guidelines, know this: marathons are hard, and the majority of athletes running them aren’t 2:30-elites—they’re runners like me and you.

In a recent development, A shoe like the Hyperion Max 4 has everything you need to make the marathon less of an hours-long suffer-fest. A nylon plate helps with snappy turnover and feels more forgiving for runners who may not have enough power running on rigid carbon. Thick slabs of PEBA DNA Gold foam and DNA Flash v2 cushion your ride, helping you endure miles of pavement pounding.

According to recent reports, two major draws of the Hyperion Max 4: the rubber coverage on the outsole and the broader platform. Super shoes tend to skimp on rubber to save weight. Though the Hyperion Max 4 weighs more than your average racing shoe, the bouncy super foams make your runs feel effortless. And the rubber outsole provides something underrated: confidence. Running in the Hyperion Max 4, you won’t fear for your life turning sharp corners or slipping over yellow strips. According to recent reports, after adding a full PEBA midsole to the Hyperion Elite 5, Brooks zeroed in on everything else in the next iteration of the shoe. The Glycerin Flex changes the paradigm of cushioning as we know it. For one thing, its stack height is comparably low at 36mm for a cushioned trainer in a sea of high-stacked super trainers reaching beyond 40mm. The tooling on the midsole is also unlike anything we’ve seen. A diagonal midfoot Flex Zone allows you to bend the shoe in half in your hands. The pliability is meant to mimic how your foot is built, allowing your feet to flex instead of being forced to comply with stiff shoe construction.

It has been revealed that the DNA Tuned cushioning is the same in the Glycerin Max and Glycerin 23. Small cells in the forefoot and large ones in the heel create a luxurious ride that absorbs shock without the foamy bulk. Lightweight and malleable, it challenges what we think when we hear cushioned trainer.

Sources indicate that “The Brooks Glycerin Flex strikes an effective balance between lightweight construction, plush cushioning, flexible midsole, comfortable fit, and outsole durability, making it well suited as an everyday trainer,” noted tester Lindsay Vuong. “The shoe transitions easily from running to gym sessions and daily wear. Recent findings suggest that brooks’s guide rails on the lateral and medial sides of the shoe act as bumpers to align ankle and knee movement. This holistic approach to stability makes the shoe a great pick for overpronators and for neutral runners who need a little support later in their runs when their form gets sloppy This is why the Adrenaline is a long run favorite.

Brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

It has been revealed that one helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

In a recent development, runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

In a recent development, at the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

For runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS debuted in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In a recent development, in 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

We always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

According to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The new DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

#68413. Breaking: Josh Kerr Claims You Probably Don’t Need Water for Runs Under 12 Miles. The Internet Had Thoughts.

Breaking: Josh Kerr Claims You Probably Don’t Need Water for Runs Under 12 Miles. The Internet Had Thoughts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant.
  • So when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from.
  • "I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr noted, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

So when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr noted, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

According to recent reports, for context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

It has been revealed that runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

Industry observers note that I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

It has been revealed that I live in Fresh York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

Industry observers note that that changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

And I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

Recent findings suggest that the Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

They're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That said, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

Industry observers note that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

Montreal-based running apparel brand Ciele certainly knows a thing or two about running in the cold, and the brand just released its second-ever Woolmark-certified collection of merino wool running apparel and accessories.

According to recent reports, the collection highlights Ciele’s two merino-based fabrics: Sorino WS, a merino-silk blend used in base layers, and Sorino W, a 100% merino fabric used in headwear. The collection includes several hats, two facemasks, and base layers for men and women. Woolmark, an independent wool authority, certifies all gear to ensure wool textiles meet industry standards for fiber content, colorfastness, and durability.

Check out some highlights from the collection below, and shop the full lineup at Ciele.com.

The beauty of this hat is its simplicity: a straightforward cap that lets merino wool's natural performance shine. Made from pure merino, it fits snugly, so it won’t shift while running, and the knit fabric naturally traps heat, vents excess moisture, and resists odors. Added bonus: This hat is machine washable (on the cold setting), and the “speedway” pattern gives it a snazzy look, too.

It has been revealed that prefer a more classic “watch cap” style beanie? Check out the VNTBeanie, also made from 100 percent merino fabric. You’ll get all the performance benefits of merino, plus the hat’s ribbed structure boosts its breathability (and looks great, too).

In a recent development, the FRDMask will help you power through icy winds and single-digit temperatures. It’s way more than a face mask: Made from a plush merino-cashmere blend, it keeps your entire head, neck, and face warm. The key is its all-encompassing design, which layers neatly under a jacket and seals cold spots that outerwear and a hat would normally leave exposed.

The HLSLongsleeve really demonstrates the value of merino as a performance fabric. Made from a comfy merino-silk blend, it regulates your temperature, breathes well, resists odors, and feels great (Ciele states the silk gives it a smooth texture and boosts its strength). The snug fit and thumbholes make it easy to layer under a jacket and gloves, but it’s also great in warmer weather—the fabric is rated UPF 30, so it protects you from sunburn when worn on its own.

Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”.

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford claims. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”.

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”.

Lunsford claims the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Industry observers note that free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

Recent findings suggest that at only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

According to recent reports, while this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

It has been revealed that the Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

According to recent reports, the unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

Industry observers note that the Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.
