Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

It has been revealed that the core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

In a recent development, hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or Upcoming Year's Eve.

Sources indicate that your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

In a recent development, the pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

Industry observers note that hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

In a recent development, go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability demonstrates for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

#68313. Industry News: What to Do About These High Interest Rates

📅 04 Sep 2023 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2559 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What to Do About These High Interest Rates

📅 04 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?
  • Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.
  • Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this new development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the important part, which is,.

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”.

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

Recent findings suggest that for most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and fresh construction alike.

It also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started newly introduced companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing new things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Industry observers note that until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

Industry observers note that so eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

And that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their prepares to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build fresh factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

Recent findings suggest that all of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:.

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

In a recent development, the reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no massive deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

Sources indicate that the stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

In a recent development, but since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

Recent findings suggest that but remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting latest highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:.

For most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:.

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:.

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

When Will House Prices Go Back Down?

According to recent reports, this is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

Sources indicate that the first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

In a recent development, thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build upcoming houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

When Will Interest Rates Go Back Down?

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

It has been revealed that remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

But a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In a recent development, in order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

Recent findings suggest that you can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:.

Sources indicate that what the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:.

It has been revealed that if you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds presently believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

And if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

The Ultimate Interest Rate Strategy Hack.

Sources indicate that I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

According to recent reports, with the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

Recent findings suggest that so to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more crucial are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller challenges of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

According to recent reports, in the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings.
  • Industry observers note that picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific.
  • Sources indicate that the core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings.

Fuel Surcharges via Partner Programs.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Strategy or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

Sources indicate that the core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points owners from strategic ones.

It has been revealed that JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:.

In a recent development, alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

Industry observers note that american AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Industry observers note that neither Alaska Mileage Initiative nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:.

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:.

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Industry observers note that go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

Sources indicate that JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Blueprint or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

In a recent development, if you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

Recent findings suggest that for Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

According to recent reports, for American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

According to recent reports, once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Proposal and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

Recent findings suggest that A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Sources indicate that booked through Alaska Mileage Proposal: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On JAL's Boeing 787-9, you'll be seated in the Sky Suite — a fully flat, forward-facing seat with a sliding door for privacy. The seat converts to a 186-cm flat bed with a proper mattress pad and duvet. The personal screen is one of the largest in the sky at 23 inches.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It demonstrates business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

In a recent development, JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

It has been revealed that this is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

According to recent reports, as emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

Industry observers note that this sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

Sources indicate that this redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

It has been revealed that for the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

According to recent reports, go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool indicates JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

It has been revealed that only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

In a recent development, call Alaska Mileage Blueprint or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

It has been revealed that JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Initiative and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

Recent findings suggest that JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

It has been revealed that not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

JAL Sky Suite business class features angled lie-flat or fully lie-flat seats depending on the aircraft, with a privacy shell, excellent Japanese cuisine, attentive service, and premium amenity kits. The service quality is consistently praised as among the best in the industry. On 777-300ER and 787 aircraft, the product competes with top-tier offerings from Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific.

According to recent reports, this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

According to recent reports, JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

#68281. Latest Update: The Arizona Experiment!

Latest Update: The Arizona Experiment!

📅 02 Nov 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.
  • Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.
  • Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The thing that drew me to early retirement is freedom, and that’s still the best part of it.

Back in 2005, the primary reason for this freedom-seeking was being able to devote my best hours to being a Dad – I had a feeling my career in tech would be too demanding to sustain once the full-time job of raising children kicked in.

Eighteen years later, wow has that guess ever turned out to be right. Early retirement has proved to be the most amazing, worthwhile adventure and it’s still just getting started. It was an astonishing thirteen years ago that I wrote to you about Little MM starting kindergarten, and now he’s done with high school.

It has given me the space to enjoy so many latest experiences, working hard and playing hard sometimes, but also slowing things way down when necessary, to deal with and grow through some real hardships.

But now, with that child-raising phase finally almost done, I’m cashing in a few of those Freedom Chips for a particularly substantial change: moving to a warm sunny place for the winter to try out a upcoming life in the walkable, bikeable, car-free community you’ve probably heard me raving about in the past: Culdesac Tempe.

So on the first of December I’ll be packing up the essential clothes, tools and gadgets, and throwing my very best mountain bike onto the Model Y to make the epic road trip across the mountains. Just in time to escape the incoming Colorado winter. And my son will be joining me for the trip!

It has been revealed that looking for updates? I have added a separate tracker page here.

Industry observers note that we’ve booked ourselves a spacious two bedroom apartment there, for four full months. Little MM will be roughly alternating his months between Arizona and Colorado so he can still have time with both parents, while I’ll be there the whole time.

In a recent development, A massive part of the fun is that this will force me to invent a whole new life for myself, away from the easy comforts of the big community and plentiful construction sites that keep me so busy here. It will be both a big change and a significant challenge, which is exactly what all of us need on a regular basis to keep life full of meaning and joy.

So What Are You Going to Do in Arizona?

The exact details are still in the works, and I’d love to hear your ideas and feedback (see the “get in touch” note below. But here’s what I’ve got so far:.

Is There a Bigger Picture To All This?

Okay, you’re onto me. If I’m going to go to the trouble of typing shit into the computer and sharing it with you, there’s usually a purpose behind it other than just journaling my own personal life, and this another one of those cases.

First of all, there are the first-layer selfish goals: I want to have the best winter ever, meet a bunch of smart new people, and I also want Culdesac to be a huge success so they will build more neighborhoods like this around the country and set an example that permanently improves the way US cities build and expand themselves in the future.

But even if you don’t care about all that, I also want to use this as a little statement about trying deliberate life changes.

Recent findings suggest that by throwing myself into a fresh community which aligns so nicely with my own values, I hope to serve as a reminder that maybe you might want to try the same thing. Or just try anything new.

In a comfortable, prosperous country like ours, some of the built in tendencies of Human nature tend to work against us, saying,.

Industry observers note that “Hey – I’ve noticed we have plenty of food and reasonable shelter and that’s good enough. So let’s just double down on the Netflix, comfort foods, and occasional luxury purchases and that will keep us safe.”.

Instead, I want you to set your life treadmill to just a bit of a steeper, healthier incline setting.

That means questioning the status quo and doing your best to keep at least one little experiment on the go in the background. Maybe that means forcing yourself to move to a better place, or taking steps towards getting a upcoming job that gives you a better work-life balance.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest move I ever made was leaving family and friends and my old job behind to move to the US, alone, at age 24. Looking back, I’m shocked I had the courage (and the organizational skills) to pull that off back then. I’ve become older and a bit slower, and so comfortable that it’s hard to imagine doing something so bold now.

Recent findings suggest that but even today 24 years later, I thank my past self every single day for doing it. My present life is an incredibly different and better thing because of that past bit of courage.

The spirit of positive experimentation might also mean starting to challenge your body more regularly – giving it harder work and exposing it to a wider swath of temperatures and movements. Or joining newly introduced Meetup groups to expand your circle of friends and experiences.

Sources indicate that it doesn’t really matter exactly what you do, as long as you point your feet in what feels like a good direction and just start moving. Create some purposeful change, which will surely feel a bit difficult, simply because change is hard. And hard things are good.

Future Arizona Neighbors: I’ll see you in four weeks!

It has been revealed that further reading: I’ve been reading books, doing life experiments, and writing about the value of strategic hardship for a while now. But the latest is a book called Dopamine Nation by the talented psychiatrist/author named Dr. Anna Lembke.

To summarize: your brain creates a baseline for happiness based on the HARDEST thing you do, and then compares everything else to that. So if you do hard things, life in general seems fantastic because of this perspective. If you eliminate all hardship, suddenly even the pleasures of life seem bland, and you live a spoiled and unmotivated life.

In a recent development, interested in stopping by for your own Mini Culdesac Experiment? They have a few short-term rentals available at rather reasonable rates (less than nearby hotels) – check em out at book.culdesac.com.

What will you do with your car?

I’m bringing the car just as a convenient electric moving truck to carry two people and four months of living supplies. Once I get there, I’ll find a safe place to park it offsite and live the full car-free lifestyle of Culdesac, much like I do when I’m here at home. I typically only use cars to carry really heavy stuff or for trips to other cities and states, but it’s even easier to accomplish this in Tempe with its location right on the light rail and with their onsite bike, scooter and even car sharing lots.

My place in Colorado is currently set up as a two bedroom house on the main floor, plus an apartment with a separate entrance on the walkout lower level. When I’m at home, I use the whole thing as one home – the apartment just makes a great place to host a fairly constant stream of visiting friends. But for the winter I’m hoping to rent out one of these spaces to a friend or trusted acquaintance who will take good care of everything, while I leave the other section free for the occasional visits I’ll be paying to this area over the winter. Aside from keeping an eye on the place, it will be a great way to practice the age-old Mustachian technique of making money while taking vacations!

What Happens at the End of March?

In a recent development, as it stands, I have no plans beyond this point. I’ll head back to Colorado for my home base, but with this being a newly introduced phase of life I’ll be layering on new adventures. Aside from the two mountain properties that I’ve been helping to build out, I may end up with an MMM Mountain Retreat of my own someday. Conclusion: ongoing thoughts on the Culdesac experiment are here: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/.

#68264. How To Afford a House These Days

How To Afford a House These Days

📅 03 Feb 2024 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:.
  • “While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.
  • I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:.

“While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.

I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.

A lot of the ideas given to young folks are “house hack” “buy a fixer upper” but that is still out of reach and/or complex to navigate with current prices and interest rates. Most townships around me do not want you to chop a house up into ADU’s or multiple units. My cousin owns 60 acres of land but he is not allowed to live on a trailer on that land.

I don’t know what the next generation of FI bloggers will offer, perhaps they are already out there and I just don’t know who they are, but I’d like to hear from them.”–.

Sources indicate that as with every critique of our ideas, I thought about this comment for a while. Tried to determine if there were any Principles of Mustachianism that were genuinely going obsolete, versus the more common side effects of Complainypants and/or Excuse-itis, two afflictions which have been weighing down our critics since the beginning.

After all, this isn’t the first time FIRE has gone obsolete. Over my retirement I’ve seen it:.

So what’s the situation right now?

Our commenter focuses on two things: the solid salaries of tech workers, and the major increases in house prices (and interest rates) in the most recent four years.

The first one — high salaries in general – is still a factor and I don’t expect that to change. Some jobs just pay more than others, and there’s a lot you can do to increase your income and switch jobs, and I’m all for it. However, ever-increasing income is not my usual focus here on MMM, because I have seen first hand that most people can waste almost any amount of income and still have very little to show for it.

In fact, the very existence of software engineers and doctors and other high earners who are my age and still feeling financial stress is proof of this: it’s mathematically impossible to earn so much for almost 30 years and not have an absolute shit-ton saved, unless you are also spending an absolute shit-ton of money the whole time.

In a recent development, so instead, we focus on how to streamline your spending and live joyfully and efficiently without compromise. We focus on reducing waste, while maintaining or even increasing all of the other benefits that come from spending money more purposefully. These skills are essential even for the highest earners, but they become even more valuable as you move down the income ladder.

So now for the second matter: housing. Does the state of housing here in 2024 screw up the whole FIRE initiative?

As with any question, let’s start by looking at the data: how much have US house prices actually risen – adjusted for inflation – since 2019?

It turns out that our own St. Louis Fed makes this extremely useful  information available here.

According to recent reports, so there’s our answer: houses “feel” about 25% more expensive right now than they did at the start of 2019 relative to the average salary and the price of everything else. Although interestingly enough,  they are only up about 10% since the last peak in early 2006, a full eighteen years ago! So housing is a blow, but not a FIRE-extinguishing one.

Recent findings suggest that however, this nationwide data masks some much bigger increases in certain popular cities, including my own: Plain old Longmont Colorado now sports a hilariously high $540,000 median home price. So houses are about triple the price they were when I started writing in 2011, which means they’ve risen much faster than the average salary. Which means houses are much further out of reach for the average person in my area.

House Shopping With Your Middle Finger.

The solution to this is the same as most other problems: to stop thinking in the way our culture likes to train us (as a victim of outside forces beyond our control) and go back to thinking like a Mustachian.

Houses are just like any other manufactured product, and as such they come at a wide variety of prices, subject to supply and demand.

According to recent reports, and just because you happen to live in a certain place (even if you were born and raised there), doesn’t mean you’ll automatically be able to afford to buy a house there. Just as a baby born upon the Apple campus in Cupertino today doesn’t automatically get a newly introduced iPhone Pro Max every year.

With every purchasing decision, you need to go through the same series of choices:.

Recent findings suggest that so when it comes to houses, you run the numbers, then decide between renting or buying or house hacking. You might start by doing the analysis right in your own city, but also keep in mind that there are lots of other cities and even countries in the world, and there are happy people living in all of them.

But Wait: I don’t want to move to a whole new place!

Industry observers note that at this point, people get defensive. We all have ties to our current location, and the stronger the ties the more difficult it becomes to consider moving.

But there’s a difference between genuine, positive bonds to a place and just plain old fear of change. So it’s my job to at least make you question your assumptions, because not doing so is what got you where you are, and it’s also what got our country where it is.

And on a country-wide basis,  I notice that our general fear of relocating creates a very irrational pattern of house prices. They are ridiculously high in some places and ridiculously cheap in others. There does seem to be a general correlation between niceness and cost, but not a perfect one (especially since everyone has their own definition of “nice”).

And that’s where the opportunity lies.

I moved to Longmont in 2005 because it met our young family’s needs at the time, at the right price with homes about $200,000. Today, at the $540,000 price level (houses average about $450 per interior square foot) it has to compete with a much broader range of cities which offer nicer amenities at equal or lower prices.

Let’s do a hypothetical search using another amazing tool: FRED’s list of the top 1000 metro areas with price per square foot, and plot some of them based on my own judgment of their desirability:.

I’m biased towards Colorado because I have so many ties there, and I also highly prioritize sunny climates. My chart suggests that if I wanted to save money, I might start looking around in Albuquerque, whereas Denver would give me a nicer life in the same price range as my current city of Longmont. And if I were willing to spend even more on housing to live somewhere even nicer, I should suck it up and move to Boulder.

Just for fun, I pulled the data from that same FRED website into a separate google spreadsheet (which I’ll share here) and sorted it by cost per square foot. Then, I highlighted a band of affordable cities with housing centered on the $100 per square foot range, which would mean a 2,000 square foot house is about $200k.

As an added bonus, I added a column to calculate the change in house prices over the past year, just in case it helps us see if a city is on the way up or getting cheaper at the moment.

A chart like this is just a starting point – you’d need to read more about any place and then go visit in person before considering a move. But the idea is to start with data, and then do some fun research based on what you learn.

The Earth Awaits: Casting a Worldwide Net.

Recent findings suggest that house prices are a valuable metric, because they influence the cost of living more than almost anything else for the typical Mustachian. After all, biking and nature are always close to free, Costcos are available nationwide, and we probably care less than average about the costs of other services like valets and salons.

Sources indicate that but there’s still plenty of value in looking at the bigger picture, considering more data points, and also being open to renting versus buying your housing. For this, I’m a significant fan of a FIRE blogger-created site called The Earth Awaits, and we can take it for a test drive right now with the following search criteria:.

My total monthly budget: $0-$6000.

Apartment type: Two bedroom (outside city center).

Temperature range: January lows not colder than 10F.

The exact parameters don’t matter too much, as long as you don’t make them too narrow. The key thing is the resulting list, which is meant to give you ideas to research further. For example, that first simple search gave me this list:.

Hey, that’s interesting. I like how the site shows the population right on the main list, because that provides a massive clue to the “feel” of a city. I personally like the feel of a 50k-200k person town, so I might look into Fayetteville, Columbia or Athens. I’ve also been to Chattanooga and really like that place – who knew it was only about as expensive as Columbus Ohio?

In the end, your physical environment – the people, access to nature, urban features and the weather patterns – is probably the most crucial factor to get right in creating a happy life. The cost of living there is only one of the factors, and definitely not the most important one.

It has been revealed that but if you choose carefully, you can probably slide yourself in the right direction along that “Nice for the Price” scale in order to get more from your life. Even if it just means making a move within your own city to live along a walking path, a little closer to work or to the people or places you care about most.

The key is just to remember that housing is like almost everything in life: It’s a choice that you get to make, and there are great rewards for putting some solid thought and effort into that choice.

Another Fun Example: Doing the Analysis on Tempe/Phoenix Arizona vs Denver.

This is a fun exercise, because I’m at the moment living in the Phoenix area (more on that here)  that is way different than the Denver metro area where I normally live. We can start with the rough measure of housing cost per square foot across each region:.

In other words, pretty close. Denver metro* is about 10% higher on average, but the variations from one neighborhood to another within any major city are much larger than that anyway.

Recent findings suggest that so the other factors are more important. Both are surrounded by beautiful mountain recreation and get lots of sunshine, but the climates are famously quite different. Denver is more compact but Phoenix has nicer towns in the foothills around the outskirts. In the end it’s just personal preference in weighting these various factors, and right now I kind of like the idea of both (Phoenix in winter but Colorado for the other three seasons).

More Adventurous: Let’s Try This in South America!

Going back to The Earth Awaits, if we repeat our earlier search but in South America, we get results like these:.

Many of these spots have nice writeups if you click the “Details” button, and if anything sounds right for you, you can go on to learn much more.

It’s true that moving to a latest country comes with all sorts of new learning experiences: citizenship and passports, laws and traditions and driver licenses, and of course having to cross an international border every time you want to return to your home country to visit family.

But guess what? If this stuff sounds daunting to you, it’s probably a sign that you need to do it more.

At its core, moving to a newly introduced place – even internationally – is just a series of relatively easy Adulting Puzzles. You type stuff into your computer, read the resulting stuff that pops up on your screen, and make the occasional phone call and visit to an official office. I had to do all the same stuff when moving from Canada to the US, alone and just six years out of high school myself.

Recent findings suggest that sure, it can feel like a “hassle” if you think of it the wrong way, but you know what’s a way, way bigger hassle? Living in a not-very-good place for life, or working an extra 15 years just to afford the higher cost of living in your current city, because you’re too scared to do a few weeks of work to make a major move to a better place.

If a rules-and-paperwork-hater like me can do it, almost anyone can.

Sources indicate that while we covered a few examples of actual places in this article, the real purpose was to explain the thought process behind deciding when and where to move. And there are many of you out there besides me who can do the same thing, but better. And we’d love to hear from you!

If you have some favorite cities and countries for good living, or useful techniques for scoping them out, please share them in the comments. I strongly believe that the more we help each other find the right place and enjoy the planet more thoroughly and more efficiently, the better off we’ll all be. So let’s get moving.

* Denver metro on the Fed site includes all the suburbs rather than just the core city which is much smaller and more expensive, but the same is true for the nicer parts of Phoenix so I figure it’s a fair comparison).

Air France-KLM Flying Blue — Monthly Promo Rewards

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing.
  • According to recent reports, picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing.

Typical Promo Biz Class One-Way.

Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

According to recent reports, picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

Recent findings suggest that flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you initiative a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Industry observers note that go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view demonstrates you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Note: Flying Blue's search only shows Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

In a recent development, do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move promptly through the next steps.

According to recent reports, from your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

Industry observers note that with miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

It has been revealed that card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's walk through a redemption that the ChooseFI community has actually executed.

The Route: Latest York (JFK) → Paris (CDG) in Business class on Air France.

Recent findings suggest that the Cash Price: A direct Air France Business class ticket on this route typically retails between $3,000 and $5,500 depending on the season. For this example, let's use a realistic mid-range price of $3,800.

According to recent reports, the Promo Reward Price: 40,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, plus approximately $60–$80 in taxes and fees. No fuel surcharges — because it's a Promo award.

The CPP Calculation: $3,800 ÷ 40,000 miles = 9.5 cents per point. That's nearly 10x what you'd get using those same Chase points for cash back at 1 cent each.

You board at JFK and step into Air France's Business class cabin — the same product that Business travelers are paying $3,800+ to access. You have a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, a curated French menu with Champagne service before takeoff, noise-canceling headphones, an amenity kit, and pajamas on longer segments. The CDG lounge is yours before departure — the Air France lounge in Terminal 2E is a genuine culinary experience, not an airport afterthought. You land in Paris rested, not wrecked.

Recent findings suggest that for a couple, you'd need 80,000 miles total — both ways would be 160,000 miles. A pair of Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve cardholders who signed up in the same year could realistically have this banked between welcome bonuses and everyday spend. Transfer from Chase to Flying Blue: instant. Time from decision to booking: under 15 minutes.

You did not pay $7,600 for two Business class tickets across the Atlantic. You paid 80,000 points and roughly $160 in fees. Those points cost you, at most, $800 in credit card spend if you valued them at 1 cent each — meaning you captured $7,440 in travel value from an $800 equivalent investment in points. That's the FI multiplier that makes this program worth mastering.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing.
